claims.text: Degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by the formation and stability of an Al/Cr-rich oxide scale.
A continuous, adherent, protective oxide scale forms on this alloy in oxidizing environments.
Additive-manufacturing-induced heterogeneity can create stress concentrations that promote oxide-scale spallation.
An imbalance in Al or Cr content can promote oxide-scale spallation.
Oxide-scale spallation can trigger catastrophic failure of the alloy.
Reducing atmospheres destabilize or reduce the protective oxide layer.
Loss of the protective oxide in reducing atmospheres accelerates void formation and internal degradation.
The as-fabricated alloy has an FCC matrix with process-induced microstructural heterogeneity.
The baseline alloy forms a moderately protective oxide scale during exposure.
Increasing the Al content will enhance formation and stability of an Al/Cr-rich oxide scale.
Oxide-scale continuity, thickness, and adhesion mediate local stress fields and interfacial integrity.
In an oxidizing atmosphere, increased Al will produce a more robust and adherent Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale.
The proposed Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale will resist deformation and spallation.
In reducing gases, oxide destabilization produces internal voids and stress concentrations that promote crack propagation and catastrophic failure.
Process-induced heterogeneities intensify the local voiding, stress concentration, and cracking effects.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the higher-Al alloy will degrade more slowly and fail later under oxidizing conditions.
Both the baseline and higher-Al alloys will undergo accelerated degradation under reducing conditions.
Under reducing conditions, the baseline alloy will fail catastrophically earlier than the higher-Al alloy.
The proposed oxide-controlled degradation behavior applies above approximately 600 degrees Celsius in strongly oxidizing or hydrogen- or carbon-monoxide-containing reducing atmospheres.
Within the stated exposure range, oxide-scale formation or demise is the dominant degradation process.
